caveats: Pinker notes that empathy alone doesn't fix this: people are poor at guessing what others don't know, so test with readers.
guidance: Picture one real reader; Buffett wrote SEC filings as if to his two smart, non-expert sisters.
Plan for the reader's task: find, understand, use.
Assume the reader knows less than you think. Pinker calls the gap the curse of knowledge.

sources.name: Pinker, The curse of knowledge (APS Observer)

summary: Clear writing starts before the first sentence: decide who will read it, what they already know, and what they must do afterward.
title: Know the reader and what they need to do

evidence: In Kimble's survey of 251 Michigan lawyers, 61% preferred the plain-language judicial opinion; an opening summary was one of the top reasons.
guidance: U.S. Army correspondence standard: bottom line up front (BLUF).
Web readers scan; NN/g recommends the inverted pyramid.
ClearMark judges praised an opening statement of purpose and required action.
summary: Lead with the conclusion, answer, or required action. Background follows.
title: Put the main point first

caveats: Nominalizations can name real abstractions (Sword). The passive is right when the actor is unknown or irrelevant (GOV.UK). Pullum showed that Strunk & White misidentified most of their 'passive' examples, so check before 'fixing'.
guidance: Diagnose: compare the sentence's subject and verb with the story's real character and action.
Turn hidden verbs (analysis, management, application) back into verbs.
Prefer active voice when the actor matters.
Zinsser: find the people behind the product or story; real people are more compelling than abstract nouns.

sources.name: Williams & Bizup, Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace

summary: The clearest sentences tell a small story: who did what. Put the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.
title: Make characters subjects and actions verbs

caveats: Gopen and Swan present these as expectations a writer can break for effect, not rules.
guidance: Put the verb right after the subject.
Start with old, linking information; end with the new.
Keep each paragraph's topics consistent (topic strings).

sources.name: Gopen & Swan, The Science of Scientific Writing (1990)

summary: Readers expect context at the start of a sentence and emphasis at the end, and the verb soon after the subject.
title: Meet the reader's structural expectations

caveats: The target is needless complexity. Precise technical terms are fine when the reader knows them or you define them.
evidence: Oppenheimer's five experiments (Applied Cognitive Psychology) found readers judged writers who used needlessly complex words as less intelligent.
guidance: Orwell's rule 2: never use a long word where a short one will do.
GOV.UK and 18F publish words-to-avoid lists (utilize, facilitate, leverage, deliver for abstract things).
Use the words your users search for.

The federal guidelines publish a 'dirty dozen' to replace first: addressees, assist, commence, implement, in accordance with, in order that, in the amount of, in the event of, it is, promulgate, this activity, utilize.
Zinsser's clutter list: 'personal friend', 'at the present time', 'assistance' for help, buzzwords, 'I might add'. CDC's Everyday Words maps about 100 public-health terms to everyday ones.

sources.name: Orwell, Politics and the English Language
Federal Plain Language Guidelines: Use simple words and phrases (archived)

summary: Choose the everyday word your reader would use: buy, help, about, start.
title: Use short, familiar words

caveats: Length is a proxy. A long sentence that is a simple list can read easily. NIH's Clear & Simple warns that writing to a readability formula can produce choppy text and drop useful familiar words.
evidence: In the studies Kimble reports, preferred plain versions averaged 18 to 19 words per sentence, down from about 25.
guidance: GOV.UK: split sentences over 25 words; no more than 5 sentences per paragraph.
Microsoft: bigger ideas, fewer words.
Federal guidelines: one idea per sentence; paragraphs of no more than 150 words in three to eight sentences, never over 250.

Sentence targets vary by source: Simply Put 8-10 words; Flesch 15 (conversational) to 20 (plain); HHS, usability.gov, and STE instructions 20; GOV.UK, Mailchimp, and STE descriptions 25. Paragraphs: HHS 3 lines on the web; Simply Put 3-5 sentences; usability.gov and STE 6 or fewer.

sources.name: Federal Plain Language Guidelines: Write short paragraphs (archived)
Flesch, How to Write Plain English, ch. 2

summary: One idea per sentence, one topic per paragraph.
title: Keep sentences and paragraphs short

guidance: SEC ladder: asset, investment, security, equity, stock, common stock, one share of IBM common stock.
Give an example for every abstract claim (Pinker).
Pinker's classic style: write as if pointing at something the reader can see.
summary: Name the thing, the number, the person. Go down the ladder of abstraction.
title: Be concrete and specific

caveats: For the objective-only version, only the satisfaction gain was statistically significant; task time, errors and memory improved but not significantly. The scannable version scored slightly lower than the control on memory. It is one 1997 study on one small site.
evidence: Morkes and Nielsen (1997) tested 51 users on five versions of a travel site. Against a promotional control, overall usability was 58% better for the concise version (about half the words), 47% for scannable, 27% for objective, and 124% for all three combined. A later rewrite of real Sun web pages scored 159% better.
guidance: Concise: about half the words.
Scannable: headings, lists, highlighted keywords, one idea per paragraph.
Objective: no marketing claims.

sources.name: Morkes & Nielsen, Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective (NN/g, 1997)

summary: Cut words, make text easy to scan, and drop promotional tone.
title: Be concise, scannable, and objective

guidance: Use 'you' (Google, plainlanguage.gov).
Present tense is simplest; limit conditionals.
Use 'must' for requirements, 'can' for options; avoid 'shall'.
Turn negatives into positives (SEC).
summary: Address the reader directly, describe how things work now, and say what is true rather than what isn't.
title: Speak to the reader: you, present tense, positive

guidance: Avoid idioms, slang, and culture-bound references (seasons, holidays, sports).
Keep helper words: that, then, of.
Put conditions before instructions.
Use one term per concept.
Keep optional words (that, the, then) and repeat verbs and subjects for clarity (Microsoft, Mailchimp).
Avoid -ing and -ed words whose role is ambiguous (Microsoft, Mailchimp, STE).
Choose words with one meaning: because, not since; after, not once (Microsoft, Mailchimp).
Controlled languages like ASD-STE100 go further: about 900 approved words, one meaning each.

sources.name: Google: Write for a global audience

summary: Plain, literal English translates and survives non-native reading.
title: Write for global readers

caveats: Over-structuring short answers is its own fault (see FMT-05).
guidance: Use numbered lists for steps and bulleted lists for other parallel items.
Use headings that describe content.
ClearMark judges repeatedly praise headings, white space, and a 'quick takeaway' at the top.
summary: Layout is part of clarity: headings that say what's in the section, numbered steps, tables for comparisons, checklists for actions.
title: Design for the task

caveats: Treat this rule set's regex hits the same way: as prompts to look, not verdicts.
evidence: Jarrett reports a study where formula-driven edits lowered scores by up to six grade levels without improving comprehension.
guidance: Use paraphrase testing, usability testing, or the plus-minus technique.
Test early and at least twice.
If you can't reach real readers, ask someone unfamiliar with the topic to read aloud and explain.
NIH: one comment that reveals a misunderstanding of a key concept deserves attention, since others may share it silently.
NIH: test comprehension, attractiveness, and acceptability; never rely on expert review alone.

sources.name: Jarrett, Readability formulas: seven reasons to avoid them

summary: The only reliable test of clarity is whether readers can find, understand, and act on the text.
title: Test with real readers, not formulas

guidance: Orwell's sixth rule: break any of these rules sooner than say anything barbarous.
Gopen and Swan: reader expectations can be broken deliberately.
Linguists (Pullum, Liberman) warn that mechanical style rules misfire.

sources.name: Orwell, Politics and the English Language
Language Log, The redemption of zombie nouns
Pullum, The Grammarians Have No Clothes

summary: Every rule here has exceptions. Clarity for this reader beats compliance with a list.
title: Treat guidelines as guidelines

evidence: HHS cites self-efficacy, a person's belief they can succeed, as a strong predictor of health behavior; small steps and relatable stories build it.
guidance: Give one main message and a call to action (CDC CCI items 1, 5).
Break behaviors into small steps the reader can start now (HHS 2.5).
Explain why each step matters and what the reader gains (CCI 13; HHS 2.4).
Stay positive: focus on tips for overcoming barriers, not the barriers (HHS 2.4).
summary: Clear isn't enough if the reader can't act. Say what to do, how, and why it's worth doing.
title: Make it actionable

caveats: The full standard is paywalled; this summary comes from the federation that drafted it.
guidance: Relevant: readers get what they need.
Findable: they can easily find it.
Understandable: they can easily understand it.
Usable: they can easily use it.
Only about 7% of the standard's roughly 485 ideas are about word choice; most are about structure, findability, and design.
summary: The ISO standard defines plain language by outcomes for the reader, not by word lists.
title: Plain language is relevant, findable, understandable, usable

guidance: Use whole numbers and natural frequencies ('1 in 4').
Explain what each number means: high or low, better or worse than expected.
Do conversions and calculations for the reader; keep denominators constant.
Prefer absolute risk to relative risk; explain any probability in words or a visual.

sources.name: CDC Clear Communication Index, Part C-D

summary: Numbers inform only when readers can interpret them without math.
title: Present numbers people can use

caveats: Written for public health materials; items like 'supporting visual' don't apply to chat replies.
evidence: CDC developed the Index from research literature and expert review for public-facing materials.
guidance: Core (all materials): one main message; at the top; visually emphasized; a supporting visual; a call to action; active voice in the main message; everyday words; lists; chunks with headings; key information first; uncertainty acknowledged.
Behavior (when asking for action): a recommendation; why it matters; how to do it.
Numbers: familiar forms; meaning explained; no math required.
Risk: nature of the risk; risks and benefits; probabilities explained in words.
Before writing, answer five planning questions: audience, audience research, objectives, format and channel, pretesting plan.

sources.name: CDC Clear Communication Index user guide

summary: A checklist makes clarity reviewable. CDC's Clear Communication Index is a research-based example: 20 yes/no items, passing score 90 out of 100.
title: Score drafts with a checklist
